lines.text: Everyone thinks a microchip brings a lost dog home. It's a chip the size of a grain of rice, with one number on it. That's it.
This is Maple. Her tag has your phone number, until she slips her collar under a fence, and the tag stays behind.
So you add the chip. No battery, no GPS. A scanner wakes it up, and it answers with one number. Now she carries it everywhere.
Then she gets out again. A shelter scans her, reads the number, and it points to nobody. You never registered it.
In one study of 53 shelters, only 58 percent of the chips they looked up were registered.
So you add the registry: her number, your name, your phone. Now that number points home.
Then you move, and get a new phone. The shelter calls your old number. Disconnected. It's the most common reason owners aren't found.
So you add updates. Change the record when you move, and check it once a year.
Then a shelter's old scanner passes over her, and stays silent. Not every scanner reads every chip.
So you add a universal scanner, the [ISO](/ˈaɪsoʊ/) chip standard, and a second pass, every time.
Now her number shows up. But which registry has it? There isn't just one.
So you add a universal lookup. Type the number once, and it points to the registry that knows her.
Months later, Maple's chip is registered, current, readable, and findable.
Then one Friday, two years later, a scanner beeps in a shelter forty miles away. Her old tag is still in the drawer. And your phone rings.
